questions.question: Explain what land use zones are and why they form in urban settlements.
questions.expected_answer: Land use is the way land is used, such as commerce, industry, residence, transport, recreation, services and open space; a land use zone is an area where one land use dominates, such as the CBD, industrial zones and residential zones, with mixed transition zones between them. Zones form because activities compete for land and have different needs. Offices and shops need accessibility, factories need space and transport links, and homes need to be away from noise and pollution. Land at the centre, where roads and railways meet, is most accessible and therefore most expensive, so activities able to pay high prices, such as banks and big shops, occupy it, while activities needing cheaper land and space are pushed outwards. Physical features and history, including apartheid planning, mean real cities do not match models exactly.

questions.question: Describe the characteristics of the CBD and explain how CBDs in South Africa have changed.
questions.expected_answer: The CBD is the commercial heart and usually the oldest part of the city, at the most accessible point where main roads and railways meet, with the most expensive land. It has the tallest buildings because developers build upwards on costly land; offices of banks, insurers and businesses; government buildings; department stores and high-order specialised shops; the main railway stations, bus terminals and taxi ranks; heavy daytime traffic and pedestrians, scarce parking, few open spaces and few residents, so it can be quiet at night. Examples are Johannesburg around the Carlton Centre, Cape Town between the harbour and the Company's Garden, Durban and Pretoria around Church Square. From the 1980s and 1990s many businesses moved to decentralised business districts such as Sandton, Umhlanga and Century City because of congestion, lack of parking, crime and ageing buildings, while old CBDs became centres of informal trade, public transport and government, and some have been renewed, for example Maboneng and Braamfontein.

questions.question: Compare light and heavy industry and explain where each is located in a city.
questions.expected_answer: Light industry makes smaller, lighter products such as clothing, food, printing, furniture and electronics, using small amounts of raw materials and energy and causing little pollution or noise; it needs good road access to customers and workers, so it is located near main roads, near residential areas, in the transition zone around the CBD or in industrial parks, in low flat-roofed buildings, for example Montague Gardens or Pinetown. Heavy industry processes bulky raw materials, uses much energy and water and makes heavy products, such as steel, refined oil, chemicals and cement; it needs a lot of cheap flat land, railway, harbour or pipeline links, water and power, and distance from homes because it pollutes, so it is on the edge of cities, along railways, beside harbours or downwind, for example Vanderbijlpark, south Durban, Saldanha Bay and Secunda. Buffer zones should separate heavy industry from homes, but apartheid planning placed some black, coloured and Indian communities, such as Merebank and Wentworth, beside heavy industry.
